articles.title: Trump admin. appeals to Supreme Court to sideline 20,000 mail ballots in California
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Monday appealed to the Supreme Court to order California election officials to set aside mail-in ballots from people it believes are noncitizens. The administration's latest move comes after a federal appeals court twice rejected the Department of Justice's request to stop California from processing the ballots of 20,000 people it suspects may be noncitizens. The Trump administration has said the ballots should not be counted until the voters' citizenship statuses can be verified, according to the Associated Press . Election officials say the list is unreliable and likely includes many citizens' names. A district judge last week warned that setting aside the ballots could disenfranchise citizens. Here's what to know. What is the Justice Department asking for? The department wants counties to "segregate — not cancel" the mail-in ballots of people on its list until their citizenship can be confirmed, according to a letter to San Bernardino County obtained by NBC News last month. That county's list included 1,133 names. It also asked counties to send identifying information about the voters on the list, including Social Security numbers and copies of their registrations, the AP reported . "Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, who signed the letters. Why does the administration say it's necessary? The Department of Homeland Security compared California's voter registration files with federal immigration records. It flagged more than 20,000 people it says are "likely" noncitizens who are registered to vote, according to a Justice Department release . Under California law, every registered voter is mailed a ballot. Voting throughout the state began in early October, and hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. In its appeal to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration asked for a "limited injunction" to set aside the ballots while the case plays out. "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote, according to the AP . Only U.S. citizens may vote in federal and state elections. "Even one noncitizen vote cancels out the ballot of an American citizen," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in the release. Essayli says the request is limited. "We're not asking California to take any drastic steps other than to sequester the ballots from the suspected noncitizens," he told Fox News last month. Why is California refusing? State officials say the federal data hasn't been verified, and that acting on it could keep eligible citizens from voting. In court filings, lawyers for the state argued that counties lack both the authority and the federal records needed to check citizenship. They also said the demand could delay certification of the results. Dean Logan, the Los Angeles County clerk, said a letter that the DOJ sent demanding help identifying noncitizens carried "a posture of intimidation and threats" just before the election, CNN reported . Sen. Alex Padilla, a Democrat of California, said the administration "has not provided any evidence for their claims of massive voter fraud." On Monday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said the appeal "reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law." Last week, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who ruled against the federal government's request, suggested that setting aside the ballots could "wreak havoc" on the election. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," he wrote. "This Court declines to be a party to such process." How common is noncitizen voting? Cases do happen, but reviews have found very few. In 2024, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican, audited the state's voter rolls and found 20 noncitizens among about 8.2 million registered voters. Federal claims have not always held up. In August, DHS told Nevada officials it had flagged about 15,900 possible noncitizen registrants. It later said that number was preliminary and that it had confirmed only 185 through manual review, CNN reported . In September, Nevada officials said their own review found that all 185 were U.S. citizens. DHS disputes that finding. What does this mean for California voters? For now, nothing has changed. No court has ordered California to set aside any ballots, and counties are still processing the ballots voters return. Voters can check the status of their ballot through the secretary of state's ballot tracking tool . articles.title: Mother identifies 20-year-old pilot killed in Florida plane crash
articles.summary: A man who was leaving the area where the private jet crashed in Palm Beach County, Fla., on Sunday sustained a leg injury, the National Transportation Safety Board said during a Monday afternoon news conference. The federal agency said that Sunday's weather conditions are a major factor in its investigation into the crash. "We have a lot of work to do on scene — this will be a several-day process," said Timothy Monville, an NTSB senior investigator. "The biggest obstacle we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway." The NTSB said it will interview witnesses to the accident as part of its investigation and encouraged anyone with relevant information, videos or audio to contact the NTSB by email at witness@ntsb.gov. People stand near a crater formed after a Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, US, November 1, 2026, in this still image obtained from a social media video. Vanessa Lara/via REUTERS Some evidence indicates that parts of the plane broke off before the private jet crashed, according to NTSB member Tom Chapman. "I want to note that if any members of the community find debris, please do not move it," he said. "Contact us or local authorities, and we will respond appropriately." He also told reporters that, according to records, a cockpit voice recorder was installed, but the NTSB doesn't know whether it was still on board. "Sometimes these things change over time," Chapman said. "Of course we're very hopeful that we can recover it. Too early to know, but that will be very important data." This is a developing story. Check back for updates. Read the original story below. A private jet bound for the Bahamas crashed in Palm Beach County, Fla., Sunday afternoon, killing all nine people on board. The Learjet 60, which had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, went down at about 12:50 p.m. ET near Cresthaven, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. Dashcam footage posted to social media by an eyewitness showed the aircraft falling toward the ground beside a road and exploding into a fireball, narrowly missing cars and homes. Duffy called the crash a "horrific tragedy" in a post on X , adding: "Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost." Air traffic control audio posted on LiveATC captured the crew's comments leading up to the crash. Someone in the cockpit can be heard saying "Mayday, mayday," reporting the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute, Reuters reported. "We're going to crash into the ground," the person said. The impact left a "massive crater" near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said at a news conference. About 600 residents were evacuated to two shelters, he said. The National Transportation Safety Board has opened an investigation, and the cause is not yet known. What we know The aircraft crashed in a residential area in Greenacres. Anadolu via Getty Images The Learjet 60 took off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. FAA records list the owner as a Delaware corporation. The National Weather Service had a flood watch in effect for the area of the crash, Palm Beach County, through Monday afternoon, with rain expected on and off across South Florida. In air traffic control audio posted on LiveATC, someone in the cockpit said they were "managing the ice" but faced "moderate" turbulence and were seeking "better rides." AP reported the crew also asked to climb. Less than a minute later, the person said "Mayday, mayday," reporting the plane was suddenly descending at 10,000 feet per minute. Seconds later, the person declared an emergency, with the descent rate reaching 20,000 feet per minute. Less than 20 seconds later, the person said: "We're going to crash into the ground," before reporting the descent rate had reached 22,000 feet per minute as the plane began to bank. Flightradar24 data showed the vertical descent rate at one point exceeded 32,000 feet per minute. The last words heard from the cockpit were "we're out of time." Accuweather reported that thunderstorms in the area produced heavy rainfall and lightning. The jet is reported to have descended at a peak of 32,000 feet per minute. Anadolu via Getty Images Driver Aki Kuusisto's dashcam footage captured the moment the jet hit the ground. "I heard a whistling noise, a big bang, and I saw a fireball," he told CBS News . "It felt like it was right next to us... you could feel it in the car." Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone injured on the ground. Authorities haven't confirmed what caused the crash or identified the people on board. Steve Arroyo, an aviation safety expert, told the Associated Press that ice and turbulence could have caused the plane to stall. What have officials said? The FAA said the aircraft departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was heading to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when the crash took place. The FAA said it was investigating and would provide further updates. DeSantis told reporters during a Sunday briefing that there were no reports of anyone on the ground being injured despite "a lot of debris" that was strewn over a "pretty significant distance." "It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis said. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road." Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the crash a "horrific tragedy" and said the FAA and Department of Transportation would be investigating the incident. What did eyewitnesses say? Anthony Blackmon, who lives around 500 feet from the site of the crash, told NBC Miami that debris from the crash struck his home. "Debris was everywhere," he said. "Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire. I've always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today." Adam Itayem told WPTV , "It sounded like a loud boom. I thought it was thunder," adding, "I saw a big crater in the ground and water coming out of the crater and a big fire too." "I heard and felt the boom," Andrew Mannino told CNN , saying he saw a "large black cloud immerse in the air," adding, "The power immediately went out and is still out." Around 600 people were evacuated by Palm Beach County authorities while federal officials investigate the crash. "We're waiting for someone to give us answers about what we're going to do, because they're not even letting us into the community to get our clothes," local resident Jesus Solorzano told WPTV. What we know about the victims Camila Corteleti identified her 20-year-old daughter, Nathalia Filgueiras , as one of the pilots of the private jet that crashed Sunday afternoon, the New York Times reported on Monday. Corteleti said her daughter earned her pilot's license at age 17. Filgueiras had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time and was working for a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale, according to her mother. Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras itsnatfilg/Threads It's not clear who the other pilot was or who was at the controls at the time of the crash, the New York Times reported. The other victims have not yet been identified. articles.title: Prosecutors announce intention to retry Lindsay Clancy for deaths of her 3 children
articles.summary: Prosecutors announced in court on Nov. 2 that they intend to retry Lindsay Clancy , the Massachusetts mother who killed her three young children. Clancy, 36, was charged with murder for killing her children Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, on Jan. 24, 2023, by strangling them with exercise bands in the basement of their Duxbury home. Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington argued she can't be held criminally responsible, Massachusetts' version of the insanity defense, because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings. Clancy's triple murder trial ended with a hung jury in early September, leaving her fate in limbo. Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said prosecutors want to retry Clancy but are waiting to decide what charges she will face until Judge William Sullivan makes a decision on three motions, including a defense motion to dismiss the murder charges. "Your honor, this would be a retrial. As to what that looks like will depend," Sprague said. "We're not at that point yet." Reddington argued prosecutors don't need to know the outcome of the motions to determine what charges they will retry Clancy on. "Why do we not know if the next trial will be murder in the first degree, or a lesser charge or no charge?" he asked. Reddington said he wants Sullivan, who is approaching mandatory retirement in June, to preside over the trial in the spring. Sullivan said requested the parties appear on Nov. 16 for another hearing. If Sullivan dismisses the defense's motion to dismiss at that hearing, the parties will then select a trial date, which Sullivan said he is hoping to schedule in March. Judge to weigh motion to dismiss The defense team pushed to have the charges against Clancy dismissed altogether and launch an investigation into the holdout juror. Defense attorney Martin Weinberg argued on Nov. 2 that retrying Clancy would violate constitutional protections against double jeopardy because Sullivan should have questioned the jury more thoroughly after receiving notes indicating one juror was refusing to follow the court's instruction on reasonable doubt, an allegation the holdout juror has denied . Sullivan interjected, noting he did question the jurors individually before declaring a mistrial on Sept. 4. Weinberg said the question Sullivan asked was “simply constitutionally insufficient to probe what was going on in that jury room." Prosecutors opposed the defense's motion , saying the mistrial was properly declared after the jury repeatedly reported it was deadlocked. Sprague argued that Sullivan could not have questioned the jurors further without probing the substance of deliberations, which is prohibited, and even if he could have done so, the appropriate response wouldn’t be dismissing the charges. "It’s not for the trial judge to choose sides in a deadlocked jury and decide," she said. Sullivan said he would take the matter under advisement. Defense argues for holdout juror probe Reddington also requested the holdout juror's phone, phone records and confidential questionnaire, among other records. Reddington asked the court to question the juror about the truthfulness of a questionnaire and his answers during jury selection, a "sworn assurance" from Sept. 3, and the use of a cell phone or receipt of outside information during deliberations. In a fiery exchange on Nov. 2, Reddington said he has evidence the holdout juror was using his cellphone and researching altruistic filicide during deliberations. Reddington said the juror was also dishonest about his criminal history on his questionnaire. Heather O'Connor, an attorney for the holdout juror, said that the mistrial decision had to be made based on what was known at the time and that these allegations came to light after the jury was dismissed. "And to be clear Juror Doe does not concede any of those allegations," O'Connor said. Sullivan said he would take the matter under advisement. Prosecutors push for gag order Prosecutors also asked the court to prohibit defense attorneys, as well as themselves, from speaking to the media in a way that would "have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceedings." Sprague argued Reddington has already made many statements that were inappropriate and "calculated to affect the public's perception of the case," including asking for a presidential pardon and saying the other jurors were "robbed" by the holdout. A defense attorney opposed that motion, arguing that such an order would constitute "prior restraint" of speech that infringes upon both Reddington's and Clancy's First Amendment rights. They said that no trial date had been set and the impact of these alleged comments on a potential future jury is "merely speculative." Sullivan said he would also take this matter under advisement. articles.title: 'A despicable betrayal': Dems incensed by Haley Stevens’s endorsement of Mike Rogers
articles.summary: On Election Day, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers will face off in what may be the marquee battle of the 2026 midterms: the race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters in Michigan. It's a contest that could decide which party controls the U.S. Senate. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats, including two independents who caucus with them. They need 51 to win back the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote.) Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible , but Democrats are also playing defense in Georgia, New Hampshire and Michigan. The Great Lakes State looks like the closest of the three. Democrats are pinning their hopes on El-Sayed , an unapologetic 42-year-old progressive who's pushing policies such as Medicare for All and ending U.S. military aid to Israel; who's willing to confront his critics and his own party's establishment; and who's vying to become America's first Muslim senator. Republicans have handed the reins to Rogers , a 63-year-old former congressman who lost an extremely close Senate race to Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin two years ago, and who has since broken with President Trump on tariffs and the war in Iran. The race has been rocked by several controversies, and the biggest came Sunday, two days before the election. Rep. Haley Stevens, the Democrat El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the primary, endorsed Rogers after the two worshipped together at Perfecting Church in Detroit. "Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today." Stevens had said days earlier that she would vote for El-Sayed, and the two were due to appear together Sunday for the first time since August. That plan collapsed after she called on him to condemn an outside group's ad tying U.S. support for Israel to grocery prices. His campaign then asked her to stay away , NBC News reported. Defending her stance, Stevens told CNN on Sunday the decision was a "weight off my shoulders" and said she had decided to switch allegiances because El-Sayed had been getting "angrier and angrier" throughout the campaign. When Stevens announced her change in support for Rogers, she maintained that she was "still a very proud Democrat." Michigan's Democratic Party chair, Curtis Hertel, fumed over the decision in a Sunday post on X , writing, "Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future." Trump told a rally in Iowa on Sunday that he'd "love" Stevens to join the Republican Party and said she'd been "very brave" to endorse Rogers. Rep. Debbie Dingell, who helped arrange the event, told the AP before the endorsement that she had called it off. "I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting," she said. "I would rather not distract from the key issues of this campaign," El-Sayed said Saturday . He attended a different Detroit church Sunday with Dingell and other Democrats, and did not address the dispute there, the AP reported. Stevens's longtime chief of staff resigned after the church visit, and more staff were expected to leave, the AP reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. On Sunday, El-Sayed spoke with reporters before a unity event with other Democrats and reacted to Stevens's endorsement, saying, "At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens." "This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from their government. I'm a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about," El-Sayed said, referring to Stevens and Rogers. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on social media on Sunday that Stevens's reversal was a "despicable betrayal." Jason Turkish, Stevens's fiancé, said last week that he would vote for Rogers because of El-Sayed's criticism of Israel's conduct in Gaza. "Every time [El-Sayed] talks about genocide, Jews get death threats," Turkish, a Michigan lawyer and registered Democrat, claimed Oct. 28 at a Rogers campaign event . "We have never seen a candidate for U.S. Senate act so recklessly toward the safety of Jews in the community as we have seen from Abdul." Further raising the stakes is the fact that Michigan couldn't be more purple, having swung to Trump in 2016, then Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, then back to Trump in 2024 — always by slim margins. Here's everything you need to know about the Michigan Senate contest. Who's winning? Here's what the polls say. Twelve polls have been conducted in October. Eleven of them have shown El-Sayed with leads ranging from 1 to 7 percentage points . New surveys from both CBS Detroit and CNN give El-Sayed a 7-point lead. The only recent poll to show Rogers ahead (by 2 points) was sponsored by a group affiliated with the former congressman . All of those polls were taken before Stevens's endorsement. To close the gap on Election Day, Rogers has been reaching out to two groups who backed Stevens over El-Sayed in the primary: Black and Jewish Democrats. In August, Stevens won a majority of Michigan's large counties with significant Black populations by an average of 8.5 percentage points . She also won Detroit with more than 60% of the vote, making El-Sayed the first Michigan Democrat since 2018 to win a statewide primary without winning the state's largest city. El-Sayed shakes hands with former President Barack Obama during a campaign event on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit. AP Photo/Paul Sancya Some members of Michigan's Jewish community also gravitated toward Stevens because El-Sayed has called the war in Gaza a "genocide" and accused Democrats who refuse to do the same of lacking the courage necessary "to stand up to Donald Trump." "Killing tens of thousands of people makes you pretty damn evil," El-Sayed told CNN in April . "It's not how evil is this one versus that one. Hamas: evil. Israeli government: evil. We can say both." It remains to be seen whether Rogers's outreach will pay off; he's also targeting more reliable Republican constituencies such as the nearly 4 million Michiganders ages 50 and older. So far, polls suggest that El-Sayed's strategy — trying to maximize his support among anti-establishment voters, Arab Americans and young voters — has put him ahead in the polls. But the polls have overestimated El-Sayed before. In the run-up to August's primary, several surveys showed El-Sayed with a double-digit lead over Stevens. The race ended up being much closer than expected, with El-Sayed edging Stevens by less than 1 percentage point . How controversial has the race been? El-Sayed's background has also made him the target of persistent attacks from Republicans, with Trump going so far as to call him a "jihadist" and accuse him of being "on the side of the terrorists." Vice President JD Vance recently said El-Sayed had "zero attachment" to the United States. El-Sayed is a U.S. citizen who was born and raised in Michigan. Rogers has claimed without evidence that El-Sayed has supported the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups. In a recent exchange at a town hall with a critic who asked him whether he denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, El-Sayed highlighted what he called the "implicit" suggestion in the question: the assumption that he'll have "dual loyalties" because of his faith. "I'm not running to be a Muslim senator," he said. "I'm running for the U.S. Senate and happen to be Muslim." After Trump referred to El-Sayed as " Mohammed " — his middle name — the Democrat responded in what has become his signature pugnacious style. "I don't care how he pronounces my name," El-Sayed said during a rally in Grand Rapids on Oct. 25. "Because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro." Trump watches a video of El-Sayed during a campaign rally on Oct. 25, 2026, in Port Huron, Mich. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Meanwhile, El-Sayed has campaigned with Hasan Piker , a Marxist streamer whom other Democrats have called antisemitic and even anti-American . "If perfectly inoffensive won elections, then Donald Trump would never have been president," El-Sayed said in April when reporters questioned his choice of allies. An independent left-wing group affiliated with Piker's uncle, commentator Cenk Uygur, also recently released an ad linking U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. The ad shows two parents shopping for their kids' lunch items; the mom tells the dad to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf. "They don't like eggs anymore?" the dad asks. "No, they like eggs," the mom answers. "But we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians." Some Democrats and Republicans have urged El-Sayed to denounce the content of the ad rather than just distancing himself from it. "That has nothing to do with our campaign," El-Sayed said of the ad. "It's certainly not what I want to be talking about right now." Who is El-Sayed? El-Sayed, 42, was born on Halloween 1984 in Rochester Hills, Mich. — a northern suburb of Detroit. His parents were immigrants from Egypt, and his first language was Arabic. He captained his high school's wrestling, football and lacrosse teams, then continued to play club lacrosse at the University of Michigan, where he majored in biology and political science. El-Sayed went on to study medicine at Michigan, Oxford University (as a Rhodes Scholar) and Columbia University, where he received his MD. Before politics, he pursued a career in public health epidemiology as a tenure-track professor, and later led the Detroit health department. In 2017, El-Sayed, then just 32, resigned as Detroit's health director to run for governor. He said at the time he was inspired by his work on the Flint water crisis . He was endorsed by prominent progressives — Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — but lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer by more than 20 percentage points. After a stint as Wayne County health director, El-Sayed decided to try again in 2026. He has since become the most prominent Democratic insurgent to channel left-wing disillusionment with politics and outrage over Israel's actions in Gaza to win his party's nomination in a state where more moderate candidates typically prevail. His argument is that even in so-called purple states such as Michigan, Democrats have a better shot at success when they pick buzzy, big-swing progressives over safe, "electable" incrementalists. Who is Rogers? Rogers was born in Livingston County, Mich., in 1963. He earned a bachelor's degree in criminal justice and sociology from Adrian College in 1985 before joining the Army. After four years of military service, Rogers joined the FBI as a special agent based in Chicago. His work with federal law enforcement focused on countering organized crime and public corruption. Rogers began his political career in 1994, when he was elected to a seat in the Michigan state legislature. He served for six years before launching his first bid for Congress. Republican Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina campaigns for Rogers in Muskegon, Mich., on Oct. 30, 2026. AP Photo/Paul Sancya Rogers was elected to the House of Representatives in one of the closest races of the 2000 election cycle, defeating Democrat Dianne Byrum by just 111 votes . During his 14-year tenure in the House, Rogers was a key conservative voice on national security and intelligence issues. He spent four years as chairman of the powerful House Intelligence Committee, much of that time focused on what he describes as "the economic and national security danger posed by China." Rogers left Congress in 2015 and quickly began a career in media. He hosted a daily syndicated radio show called Something to Think About with Mike Rogers and worked as a commentator for CNN. Rogers returned to run for the Senate in 2024. Roughly six months after that loss, he announced his plan to run again in 2026. Rogers is a conservative Republican on most issues — including abortion, immigration and transgender rights — but his opinion on Trump has shifted through the years. Over the past few weeks, Rogers has retreated from his early support for the president on two key issues: calling for Trump to end the "tariff war" with Canada and saying the conflict in Iran should also "end quickly." articles.title: Judge dismisses complaint against ex-FBI officials accused of lying about Hunter Biden
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Monday dismissed a criminal complaint against two former FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden, citing what he said was “weaponization” of President Donald Trump's Justice Department just before the midterm elections. In a scathing, hourlong ruling read from the bench, U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said the investigation that produced the charges against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides was rushed, conducted at the behest of Trump and FBI Director Kash Patel and dogged by “critical mistakes" that require the dismissal of the case. “I am deeply troubled by what has happened here in this case," Faruqui said. “What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization.” The ruling may not bring a permanent end to the matter because the Justice Department still has the option of pursuing an indictment, even though it has struggled during the Trump administration to persuade grand juries in the nation’s capital to return indictments in politically charged prosecutions like this one. In the meantime, it nonetheless amounts to a resounding rebuke of a department the judge said could have sought an indictment at any time but instead opted for transparently political purposes to file a criminal complaint in the immediate run-up to Tuesday's midterm voting . “I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend that I cannot read a calendar,” Faruqui said, alluding to the proximity of the charges to the elections, which will determine control of Congress for the last two years of the Republican president's second term. Prosecutors had accused the two former FBI officials of falsely downplaying to Congress their knowledge of investigations into President Joe Biden's son and of a laptop the younger Biden dropped off at a computer repair shop in Delaware in 2019. But Faruqui said the Justice Department had failed to establish in its complaint that any statements made during 2023 testimony were intentionally false and had affected lawmakers' investigation of Hunter Biden or that the former officials had any motive to deceive. “Without motive, without direct evidence, I have nothing" to go on, Faruqui said to establish probable cause needed to affirm the complaint. Lawyers for Floris, who after the ruling hugged supporters outside the courtroom, said the “so-called prosecution was nothing more than a politically motivated smear campaign aimed at scoring political points before the midterm elections." “The charges brought under the clearly discredited authority of the Department of Justice should never have been brought in the first place,” the attorneys said in a statement. The judge identified a political motive and ‘critical mistakes’ The dismissal followed a dramatic three-day hearing last week in which an FBI agent who had been assigned to investigate the case conceded that the inquiry had been regarded around his office as something of a “witch hunt” and that he himself had regarded it as a “huge distraction” from his ordinary case work. The agent, Bryan Witt, said the investigation had been opened one day after a primetime election security speech from Trump in which he rehashed longstanding grievances over his 2020 loss to Joe Biden, a Democrat. He said the investigation was assigned to his Kansas City, Missouri, office and that Patel, a close Trump ally, demanded and received constant updates — something Witt said was unusual. Recounting the pressure to deliver that Witt said he operated under, Faruqui faulted the Trump administration for a rushed investigation that undermined the results. “The rush to charge led to critical mistakes,” he said. Among the errors the magistrate cited was that the complaint said that the two officials had provided sworn testimony to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee when they were not under oath. The judge's concerns about the case were apparent almost immediately, when he raised questions about why the Justice Department had charged the case through a criminal complaint — which is more typically done when investigators have a pressing need to take a defendant into custody — as opposed to an indictment that requires a grand jury's approval. “It is self-evident that the U.S. attorney's office is avoiding taking this case to a grand jury,” Faruqui said. Last week, the Justice Department failed to secure a grand jury indictment against Cassidy Hutchinson, a former White House staffer who provided dramatic but disputed testimony against Trump before a House committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol insurrection . Then, at a preliminary hearing last week, Faruqui criticized the Justice Department for filing overnight an amended complaint with an additional criminal charge straight to the docket instead of first clearing the new charge with the court — something he said he had never seen before. The case concerns years-old questions about a laptop The case centers on a laptop that the Justice Department says Hunter Biden abandoned at a Wilmington, Delaware, computer repair shop in 2019. The laptop's existence was publicly disclosed in October 2020 with a New York Post story that reported on some of the laptop's contents. Floris and Benavides were leaders of the FBI Foreign Influence Task Force, or FITF, which was set up to monitor efforts by other countries to meddle in American politics but was disbanded last year by the Trump administration after years of Republican criticism. The Justice Department accused them of falsely downplaying their knowledge of the laptop when they appeared before the House Judiciary Committee as it was conducting its own investigation of Hunter Biden's business dealings. A prosecutor argued last week that the former officials may have had an incentive to minimize their knowledge of the laptop because Joe Biden was president at the time they were questioned and to distance themselves from the fact that the FITF did not publicly correct a narrative from some Democrats and former intelligence officials that the laptop might have been connected to Russian disinformation. Trump’s then-intelligence director, John Ratcliffe , said after the laptop was publicized that there were no signs of foreign involvement. Defense lawyers challenged that characterization. Faruqui said prosecutors had not identified a plausible motive for why the former officials might have made intentionally false statements. articles.title: Which party has a better chance of winning the midterms? What the final polls say.
articles.summary: The 2026 midterm elections are tomorrow. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to geek out over some cold, hard data. The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. And they have been wrong before . Yet time is almost up — and the stakes on Nov. 3 couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too. The state-by-state midterm landscape has reached its final form — and the polling trends are clear. Here are the numbers on the eve of Election Day. The generic congressional ballot Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds). You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading. History is helpful here, courtesy of the RealClear Politics polling average : At this point in 2022 — after nearly two years of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans had a small but significant lead (2.5 percentage points) on the generic ballot. On Election Day, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House. At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 7.3 points on the generic ballot. The next day, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But by the eve of Election Day, voters had clearly broken against Democrats. In 2014, a Republican polling lead of 2.4 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House; in 2010, those numbers were 8.7 points and 63 seats, respectively. So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — nearly 9 percentage points , on average. And that margin has held steady over the last month. Democrats might not reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House. Advantage? Democrats. 12 specific Senate races National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible. In the states where Dems are playing defense — Michigan, Georgia, New Hampshire — their leads are solidifying; meanwhile, red states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina seem increasingly competitive. Here are the 12 races to follow: Maine (Republican seat) Republican Susan Collins (incumbent) Democrat Troy Jackson What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena University poll shows Jackson ahead by 6 . Michigan (Democratic seat) Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress) Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director) What the latest polls say : Eighteen polls were conducted in October. Seventeen of them showed El-Sayed in the lead, by anywhere from 1 to 9 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena University survey gives El-Sayed an 11-point lead ; new polls from YouGov ( El-Sayed +4 ) and Research Co. ( El-Sayed +2 ) show smaller margins for the Democrat. Ohio (Republican seat) Republican Jon Husted (incumbent) Democrat Sherrod Brown (former senator) What the latest polls say : Brown has edged Husted in nearly every poll conducted since the first week of October, with margins ranging from 2 to 6 percentage points. The final New York Times/Siena University survey gives Brown a 6-point advantage . Georgia (Democratic seat) Democrat Jon Ossoff (incumbent) Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with October polls putting him ahead by an average of 9 percentage points . A new Echelon Insights survey gives Ossoff a 15-point lead . North Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman) Democrat Roy Cooper (former governor) What the latest polls say : Cooper leads by nearly 11 points, on average . Final polls from YouGov and East Carolina University show him ahead by 11 points and 9 points, respectively. New Hampshire (Democratic seat) Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator) Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative) What the latest polls say : Pappas and Sununu were previously trading leads in polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But Pappas appears to have opened a substantial lead — average margin: 7.5 percentage points — over the last month. The final University of New Hampshire survey shows him ahead by 12 . Alaska (Republican seat) Republican Dan Sullivan (incumbent) Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Surveys conducted in October show Peltola leading by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena Universty poll gives her a narrow 48-46% advantage . Iowa (Republican seat) Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress) Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete) What the latest polls say : Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries . The final YouGov and New York Times/Siena University polls show Turek ahead by 1 point; GrayHouse and co/efficient polls show Hinson leading by 2. Texas (Republican seat) Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general) Democrat James Talarico (state legislator) What the latest polls say : Nearly every poll conducted this fall has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins were small — between 2 and 6 points. But the Democrat seems to be closing strong: final polls from Atlas Intel and the New York Times/Siena University show him ahead by 6 and 7 points, respectively. Nebraska (Republican seat) Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor) Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support) What the latest polls say : Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent nonpartisan results suggest Osborn could be competitive, and a couple of Osborn-affiliated polls show Ricketts and his independent challenger trading small leads. An Echelon Insights poll released on Tuesday shows Ricketts ahead by 1 point; a New York Times/Siena University survey released on Saturday gives Ricketts a 6-point lead. Kansas (Republican seat) Republican Roger Marshall (incumbent) Democrat Adam Hamilton (Methodist pastor who previously considered an independent run) What the latest polls say :  Only one survey conducted over the last month shows Marshall ahead (by a single point). The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points). A new CNN poll has Hamilton up by 4 ; a new Emerson College survey puts him ahead by roughly the same amount . On Friday, the Washington Post released a poll showing Hamilton lapping Marshall by about 10 points. But the paper questioned its own results , noting that Republicans responded at much lower rates than Democrats. The final New York Times/Siena University survey shows Hamilton ahead by 5 . South Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Darline Graham (incumbent, appointed to replace her brother Lindsey Graham after his death in July) Democrat Annie Andrews (pediatrician and former U.S. House candidate) What the latest polls say : Graham held a narrow lead in most fall surveys . But it was small enough — between 1 and 3 percentage points — that Democrats are now targeting South Carolina as well. A partisan poll released on Friday gave Andrews a 5-point advantage; a new New York Times/Siena University poll shows the two candidates essentially tied. Advantage? Democrats. They've been consistently gaining ground over the last month, to the point where they are now favored to flip the Senate — unless the polls are wrong. Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability President Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Greenville, N.C., on Oct. 20. KENT NISHIMURA via Getty Images To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle. At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 59.4% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 38% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -21.5% — near his all-time low. Here's a sampling of Trump's latest net approval numbers from a few top pollsters: New York Times/Siena University : -26% American Research Group : -38% CNN/SSRS : -35% Reuters/Ipsos : -35% Again, history can provide perspective . In late-October 2018, Trump was about 10 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November. According to the New York Times , Trump has the second lowest approval rating heading into the midterms since 1946, behind only Harry Truman. George W. Bush's approval rating was higher at this point in 2006 — a year in which Democrats went on to flip the House and Senate. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 70% disapprove and 25% approve. That's a 45-point gap. In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency  — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection. Advantage? Democrats. articles.title: Man completes 31,000-mile walk around the world and returns to mom’s house
articles.summary: HULL, England (AP) — Karl Bushby embraced his weeping mother in his arms Monday as he returned to his northern England home to complete a 28-year odyssey to walk around the world . “Where have you been?” his mother, Angela, asked as he arrived outside the home he left in 1998 that was now decked with a banner saying “Welcome Home Son.” He didn’t need to tell her. Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, on Nov. 1, 1998, and walked 31,000 miles (50,000 kilometers) across four continents and 30 countries to get home. He navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel to avoid taking a boat or plane — or any transport — to propel him forward. He vowed not to return until he could complete the journey on foot. It was an eye-opening adventure full of danger and drudgery that was interrupted for years at a time by the unexpected: the 2008 financial crash that sapped funding from sponsors, the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and mountains of bureaucratic red tape to get across international borders. A trek made possible by kind strangers On the final day of the journey, Bushby pushed his cart toward a hero’s welcome at City Hall before setting off for the last stretch to see his mother. “Sorry to keep you waiting,” he joked to the crowd of hundreds who cheered his arrival. “Is that it, is it done?” The ex-paratrooper said he looked like he was 10 years old when he left his mother's row house at the age of 29. He returned at 57 — softer, grayer and weathered, but far more worldly. “They say it takes a village but literally it took a world to get me here,” Bushby said. “The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation states to get me back here today. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth.” The idea started with a birthday card from his dad Bushby had a thirst for adventure, but his mission only came into focus when his father, Keith, sent him a birthday card in the mid-90s. His dad, an army veteran himself, mentioned an argument two special forces troops had about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge, believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels. Perilous jungles, scorching deserts and frozen tundra slowed him down, but bureaucratic holdups brought his adventure to a halt for long periods. Bushby originally calculated the distance could be covered in about five years, but he knew that was unrealistic. “You just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that,” he said. “We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years.” Danger on land and sea followed by border problems He dodged Colombia's armed conflict in the dangerous Darién Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America in 2001, and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama. After being airlifted to safety during the 56-mile (90-kilometer) Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, they started again and faced a standoff with a polar bear, survived near-death plunges into freezing waters and almost lost all their supplies when their sleds plunged in the sea. After managing the rare crossing, the pair were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally. It took Bushby almost 10 years to make his way through Russia in fits and starts because of visa struggles and weather that only allowed travel a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork. Family firsts and a long-awaited reunion Bushby has met several times over the decades with family members who have met up with him on his journey. He was greeted on the beach in Dover by his father and brothers after crossing the channel last month. He reunited with Adam, his 36-year-old son from an early marriage whom he had rarely seen, and he met his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time, which he said was amazing. Bushby hadn't seen his mother in a decade, setting the stage for an emotional and somewhat awkward reunion captured amid a throng of cameras and a documentary film crew. “Behave yourself, mother,” he joked, as his mother wrapped her arms around him and wept. “Get yourself together.” He said he had long tried to imagine that moment he would return to find his mother at the gate where he left her so long ago. He said it was an emotional reunion that was “one great, big, blurry mess” he was trying to process. “It was kind of almost shocking to see my mother after so long,” he said at a news conference later. “She’s changed a lot. We’ve all changed a lot in that time.” Next steps for a man who walked millions In the final days of his trip, Bushby spoke of his anxiety over the trip ending, not knowing what he would do next and coming to terms with having to live in his mom’s basement. “It’s like stepping across the event horizon into a black hole,” he told The Associated Press. “I have no idea what’s about to happen in my life.” There will be plenty to keep him busy. Six speaking engagements are scheduled in the next two months, a sequel to his memoir “Giant Steps" is due and German filmmaker Werner Herzog is making a documentary on his trek. He expects to struggle with the ups and downs other adventurers have experienced after long journeys. “The only way I think, you know, you get over that is just get another mission, another passion and get busy,” he said. “That’s what I intend on doing.” ___ Melley reported from London. articles.title: Iran official says 'the ball is now in the U.S.' court' regarding peace talks
articles.summary: Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway. Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities. See the most recent developments below. Latest Developments Nov  2, 7:13 AM Nations that help US, Israel to attack Iran will face 'consequences,' Tehran says During his press conference on Monday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baqaei said that Tehran is prepared "for any eventuality" amid the ongoing conflict with the U.S. and Israel, adding that any potential resumption of attacks by the combatants would draw in other regional nations. "The war is ongoing right now, as we speak. The economic siege of Iran and the threats against Iran are themselves part of the war that has existed over these eight months. We must be prepared for any eventuality, because what is at stake is the defense of the homeland, the defense of the territorial integrity and dignity of a country with a civilization thousands of years old," Baqaei said. "Any party" that assists the U.S. and Israel "in any aggression must not assume it is safe from the harm of Iran's decisive response," Baqaei said. In the ongoing talks over a potential peace deal, Baqaei said that Iran's "demands have been expressed very clearly and transparently." "No final agreement can begin, and the Strait of Hormuz cannot be reopened or safe, unless the U.S. naval blockade ends, Iran's demands are respected and Iran's legitimate requests are implemented; then we can talk about continuing the process," he said. -ABC News' Victoria Beaule Nov  2, 5:16 AM Iran warns of 'powerful response' to any renewed attack Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baqaei said in a press conference on Monday that any "act of aggression against Iran, by any means, will be met with a powerful, immediate and comprehensive response," amid concerns of renewed U.S.-Israeli strikes on the country. Baqaei said that "the ball is now in the U.S.' court," with regards to negotiations for a resolution to the war. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi was in Qatar over the weekend "to facilitate an exchange of messages between Iran and the United States through the mediation of Qatar," Baqaei said. -ABC News' Victoria Beaule Nov  2, 3:38 AM Ships attacked in Strait of Hormuz, Persian Gulf, UKTMO says The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre reported two attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf that occurred on Sunday. The first incident occurred on Sunday afternoon, when a merchant vessel in the Strait of Hormuz reported that another ship in the area was "struck by an unknown projectile," UKMTO said. On Sunday night, a tanker traveling southeast through the Persian Gulf "was struck by two unknown projectiles" while around 72 nautical miles east of the coastal Saudi city of Ras al-Khafji, UKMTO said. Nov  2, 3:07 AM Trump says he had 'very good' call with Netanyahu President Donald Trump confirmed on Sunday that he spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday. The president did not offer any detail on the call, beyond describing it as "good" and confirming they discussed the war with Iran. "We had a very good talk," Trump said. -ABC News' Nicholas Kerr Nov  1, 10:59 AM Tehran prepared for 'defense and diplomacy,' Araghchi says Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran is prepared for "both defense and diplomacy," amid ongoing talks between Iranian and Qatari representatives over a possible peace deal to end the U.S.-Israeli war against the country that began in February. “Our armed forces have a very specific mission, and by leveraging the lessons learned from the two previous wars, they are now significantly stronger than before,” Araghchi said, as quoted by the semi-official Mehr News Agency. -ABC News’ Rashid Haddou Nov  1, 6:42 AM Tehran officials vow 'immediate' response to any fresh attacks Iranian Defense Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi warned in a statement on Sunday that Tehran is "committed to strengthening combat readiness and ensuring an immediate, effective and proportionate response to any threat, anywhere, without geographical limits." Akhlaghi's statement -- which was published by the semi-official Mehr News Agency -- came amid concerns that the U.S. and Israel may soon resume strikes on the country amid stalled peace negotiations. President Donald Trump has said that the U.S. will not launch any new attacks until after the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Several other top Iranian officials and commanders have issued similar warnings. In comments published by Mehr on Sunday, Mohsen Rezaei -- the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a key military adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei -- said any new strikes would be met with "devastating" retaliation." Nov  1, 3:04 AM Trump says US not in 'a hurry' to agree deal President Donald Trump said on Saturday during a Halloween event at Mar-a-Lago that the U.S. has no hard timetable regarding negotiations with Iran over a possible deal to end the ongoing war with Iran. "We're not in that much of a hurry from the standpoint that we've knocked out their navy," Trump said. "We've knocked out their air force, we've knocked out their anti-aircraft, we've knocked out almost every piece of military equipment they have." Trump also said the U.S. had "knocked out" much of Iran's manufacturing capability and nuclear sites. "We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in ten minutes." articles.title: Democrats eye a return to power. Division over how to handle Trump is already brewing.
articles.summary: Democrats are expecting to win big on Election Day, but disagreements are already erupting among them over how aggressively to target President Trump for what they say are abuses of power and corruption. Democratic lawmakers and strategists are divided over whether to push another impeachment against Trump. Senators and leaders in the House are generally opposed to advancing a third impeachment of Trump that has virtually no chance of picking up 67 votes in the Senate — the number of votes needed to convict. A senior Senate Democratic aide warned there is little “appetite” for holding a third Trump impeachment trial in the Senate, after previous impeachment efforts in 2020 and 2021 failed to impact Trump politically. Democrats agree there need to be investigations of Trump and his allies next year to hold them to account, but there is little consensus over what to prioritize, according to Democratic strategists and aides. But some senior lawmakers are warning that the party can’t get so wrapped up in tracking down the misdeeds of the president and the administration that they get pulled into too many directions or lose sight of addressing high prices and ending the war in Iran — two of the top issues of this year’s election. “I don’t think we can ignore it,” said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) of the need to investigate alleged corruption in the Trump administration. “More than 90 percent of voters think that government has been corrupted. We just have to be thoughtful and strategic about where investigative work goes and not allow that to distract us from solving fairly immediate cost problems that American families feel,” he said. Whitehouse would become chair of the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee if Democrats win control of the Senate. To keep their hoped-for new House majority — and possible Senate majority — from getting sucked into solely partisan battles with Trump over what has already transpired, Democratic leaders in Congress are mapping out positive agendas for the first 100 hours, the first 100 days and the first year of their new majorities, according to sources familiar with internal discussions. Yet the desire among Democratic lawmakers to inflict retribution on Trump is strong. Some want to delve further into the Jeffrey Epstein sex-trafficking scandal to probe whether the Justice Department violated the Epstein Files Transparency Act by withholding or improperly redacting documents. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who would return to the role of majority leader if Democrats capture the Senate, created a special Senate working group in February to plumb Epstein-related information held back from the public by the Trump Justice Department. “We are demanding that the Department of Justice and the FBI preserve records on what transpired behind the scenes. We want to know who was involved in the decision to hide the truth,” he declared. Other Democrats want to prioritize investigations of the Defense Department and the awarding of lucrative contracts linked to Donald Trump Jr. Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) sent a letter to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth earlier this year demanding information about decisions at the Pentagon to give loans and contracts to companies “associated with the president’s son” that may have had “conflicts of interest.” Some Democrats are pushing for investigations into the Trump family’s massive investments in the crypto industry; the president’s pardon of Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao, who pleaded guilty to violating money laundering law; and whether crypto investments provided an avenue for foreign interests to influence the president. “We’re going to have to do voluminous oversight work because there is rampant corruption in this administration, and we need to get to the bottom of it,” said Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.). Some Democrats want to investigate Trump’s pardon record more closely and scrutinize donations that wealthy individuals and families made in hopes of receiving clemency. The New York Times reported that Alina Habba Mildon, one of Trump’s former lawyers, earned $50 million to help secure a pardon for the member of a wealthy Venezuelan family, among other duties. A Democratic strategist and former House leadership aide said Democratic leaders are looking at a wide array of issues to investigate when they take back the Speaker’s gavel in January. “Everything from corporate America and their ties to the Trump administration, Epstein, immigration,” said the strategist, noting that Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who would take over as chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has been outspoken about investigating conditions at Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities and immigration enforcement activities more generally. “They’re going to spend their time looking at a variety of issues,” the strategist added, noting Democrats are “running on affordability and corruption” in the midterm election. The House-aligned Democratic strategist said there’s little desire among House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries's (N.Y.) leadership team to move toward another impeachment proceeding, even though there are rank-and-file members in the Democratic caucus who want to. “I’ll tell you right now that I have not heard about impeachment, not for Trump,” the source said. The strategist said Democratic leaders instead are eyeing a lower-key strategy to hamstring the Trump administration by tying up Cabinet and other senior officials in oversight hearings. “That’s what they’re elected to do, to constrain Trump and to ensure that they try to get some of their agenda passed and signed into law,” the strategist said. Beyond investigations, Democrats are threatening to make it much tougher for Trump to make appointments to the federal judiciary and the executive branch if they win control of the Senate. And they’ve threatened to cut off funding for the war with Iran if Trump doesn’t bring the conflict to a swift conclusion. Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), who is set to become the next Senate Democratic whip, has warned that getting bipartisan majorities to vote for bills to authorize and fund the Pentagon will be “extremely difficult” if the war drags on. Some Democrats, however, argue that Trump still needs to face accountability for trying to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election or for mishandling classified documents and conspiring to obstruct justice related to those documents after leaving office in 2021. “Donald Trump’s alleged crimes still have not been given justice. There’s been no justice yet for these alleged crimes, which are just so deeply serious, and were stopped midway in the criminal justice process,” said Blumenthal, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee. “I still feel there needs to be some reckoning,” he said. Blumenthal would be poised to take over as chair of the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations if Democrats win control of the Senate this week. Other Democrats say they want to investigate what they say has been a “corrupt relationship” between the Trump administration and wealthy special interests over the past 20 months. Murphy says he wants to know more about “an $8 million donation made by R.J. Reynolds to the administration that resulted one week later in flavored vapes being made legal for kids.” “We should get to the bottom of the corrupt relationship that exists between corporations in this country and the Trump administration,” he said. articles.title: Republicans privately criticize Trump amid fears of major midterm election losses
articles.summary: Republicans are already privately blaming President Donald Trump as they brace for losses on Tuesday. Even as they race to distance themselves from his actions on tariffs, the unpopular Iran war and his mass deportation agenda, few have been willing to criticize him publicly — a clear sign of just how powerful Trump's grip remains on the GOP. But interviews with roughly a dozen candidates, campaign officials and lawmakers reveal they're acutely aware of who, exactly, put them on the back foot this entire cycle. "There was a point earlier this year where we really felt like we could defy history," said one House Republican, who, like others in this article, was granted anonymity to candidly discuss midterms dynamics. "And then Trump bombed Iran. And it was just one thing after another.” Republicans are tied or trailing in polls in numerous critical battlegrounds and expecting to lose some once-secure red seats. And Trump's unfocused closing message — including repeated comments about male candidates' physical appearances — has further frustrated an already on-edge party. “I think Jon Husted's ass and Nicki Minaj's is a great closing message,” T.W. Arrighi, a Republican strategist working on the South Carolina Senate race and others, said sarcastically in an interview on The Conversation with Dasha Burns . “You’ve got to take the good with the bad with Trump, unless you want to drive yourself crazy every day.” “People are gonna go after the president. The buck stops with him. His approval ratings aren't great,” he added. Privately, some Republicans are even harsher. “At least when Barack Obama was president, he only screwed his enemies, never his friends,” said a second House Republican. The White House defended its involvement in the war with Iran, tariff regime and approach to immigration enforcement. Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that Trump “is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.” One White House official, granted anonymity to speak candidly, called the blame game “an asinine adventure” and said Trump “has obviously left it all on the field.” If the bottom falls out for the GOP on Tuesday, the quiet calls assigning him blame may turn into a public shanking as Trump nears the lame-duck stage of his presidency, Republicans refocus on how to win voters back for 2028 and jostle for their own spots in the party’s future. “I'm not sure what the Republican Party looks like in six months. Look, a lot of Republicans have held their tongues. A lot of Republicans who have real problems with the way things have gone the last two years have been good soldiers,” said a Republican strategist involved in competitive midterm races across the country. “But what happens if we lose 35 House seats and six Senate seats?” “We all know who the problem is. It’s Trump. And do we continue down a path of losing?” the strategist added. In Georgia, some Republicans have already warned that low early voting turnout in rural parts of the state could drag down their entire ticket. "If you live in rural Georgia, you're going to be disproportionately hurt by higher — especially diesel — prices,” said Jason Shepherd, the former GOP chair of suburban Cobb County. “The promise of the great Trump economy has not materialized." Top Hill Republicans have worked behind the scenes for months to try to alleviate some of the political fallout from Trump’s election year policy moves, including arguing to White House officials that Maine Sen. Susan Collins and Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers could lose their races if the administration didn’t reach an off-ramp from the trade war with Canada, according to three Republicans with direct knowledge of the matter. Eventually, Trump agreed to roll back some tariffs and add new ones in a boost to Collins. Republicans also pressed for the White House to undo some of Trump’s other controversial moves, like his executive order to import more foreign beef that has riled ranchers and farmers in red states like Kansas, Iowa and Texas. But that relief never came. "Republicans have always been aware of the historical midterm precedent, and that's why we're barnstorming the country to tout the president's achievements on cutting taxes, securing the border, and lowering drug costs,” said Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee. “Any anonymous strategist who says the president is not helpful in turning out Republican voters has no idea what they're talking about, and their candidates should request a refund for their shoddy consulting services." But Trump’s actions, Republicans say, are hitting different parts of the country hard. The Iran war, they argue, was a significant blunder from Trump that has multiplied Democrats’ paths to power in both the House and Senate by driving fuel and fertilizer costs up — most notably impacting races across the Midwest. The White House’s tariffs regime has been a major concern in battlegrounds on the Canadian border like Maine and Michigan. Hardline immigration enforcement that has resulted in the deportation of thousands has hurt especially in heavily Latino border states like Arizona and Texas, and the cancelling of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Venezuelans has enraged South Florida voters. Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, a Miami Republican, warned the president in a campaign ad earlier this year that his immigration tactics had gone too far. “Trump won Miami, and yet he went to the place that gave him the biggest support, and kind of just fucked everybody over if we're being honest.” said one Florida-based Republican operative. New results from The POLITICO Poll show that Republican midterm voters are split over who they would blame if the GOP performs worse than it did in 2024: A sizable 29% blame Trump for making the GOP less popular, while 30% said it is because Trump himself is not on the ballot. Fourteen percent said it would be because the Democratic Party has become more popular, while roughly one in four said they don’t know. Some in the party question whether Trump’s last-minute campaign travel across the country and the millions of dollars his political operation has poured into battleground states will even be enough. They see him as more absorbed in protecting his legacy than making actionable policy changes to help his party stay in power. “He cares more about the ballroom than he cares about Republicans winning the midterms,” said a third Republican strategist working in battleground races. “He wants the Nobel Peace Prize, these big legacy-defining things seem to be taking up more of his attention than actually being president.” A fourth GOP operative working on midterms races has a curt message if Republicans lose big: “Thank you, Donald Trump." Dasha Burns contributed reporting. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/02/republicans-blame-trump-midterms-2026-01143980

articles.title: 哈塞特淡化AI债务风险：行业资金充裕，不存在全面抛售风险
articles.summary: 白宫国家经济委员会主任凯文·哈塞特淡化了市场对AI基础设施建设融资风险的担忧。他表示，AI行业实际上拥有一个资金非常充裕的生态系统，即使部分企业面临债务压力，市场上也存在资金实力雄厚的企业，可能愿意在相关公司陷入困境时出手。 哈塞特周一接受CNBC采访时表示， 近期科技股大幅下跌，并不意味着AI行业面临全面抛售风险。 他承认，一些企业可能背负了大量债务，确实值得关注，但与此同时，行业内有不少资金实力雄厚的公司，既持有相关企业的股权，也持有债权，可能伺机收购或提供资金支持。 “这个生态系统里有太多现金了，我认为人们应该对此感到放心。”哈塞特说。他同时表示，经历此前的大幅上涨后，市场有时确实需要出现一定回调，但他认为完全不存在全面抛售的风险。 哈塞特的表态正值AI交易遭遇新一轮调整之际。上周，科技股抛售加剧，谷歌，英特尔业绩指引不及预期、，投资者对AI基础设施投入回报的担忧加剧。 市场重新审视AI投资回报 近期市场对AI行业的担忧，已经从企业能否维持高速增长，逐渐转向巨额资本开支能否转化为足够的收入和现金流。 尽管大型AI投资者的最新财报显示云计算业务仍保持强劲增长，但投资者的关注点正在转向数据中心建设成本，以及这些投入对企业自由现金流造成的压力。随着资本开支持续攀升，市场对大型科技公司的投资回报要求也在提高。 此前公布的财报显示，Alphabet、亚马逊和Meta均进一步提高了AI相关投资计划。与此同时，部分企业的自由现金流已经受到明显挤压，令投资者开始质疑持续扩张所需资金将从何而来。 AI融资压力显现 AI基础设施融资市场正出现越来越明显的压力。为数据中心和芯片建设提供资金的部分债券及贷款收益率已经升至两位数，银行也越来越难以将相关融资风险转移给保险公司和其他投资者。 市场尤其关注被称为“新云”（Neocloud）的专业AI算力服务商，这类企业通常需要先投入巨额资金建设算力设施，再通过出租算力逐步回收成本。 据英国金融时报，AI行业融资越来越依赖债务，2026年AI相关债务发行规模可能超过6000亿美元，达到2024年的约10倍。随着全球利率水平上升，资本成本正在成为AI基础设施投资无法回避的约束。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 华尔街严阵以待美债发行多年来最大调整：长债或提前减量，短债融资占比面临考验
articles.summary: 美国财政部即将公布新一季度再融资声明，华尔街正密切关注美国国债发行策略是否迎来2024年以来最大调整。 在美国财长贝森特近期多次释放干预债市、压低长期收益率信号后，市场普遍预期，财政部可能调整维持国债发行规模稳定的政策指引，为未来削减20年期和30年期长期国债发行铺路，同时更多依赖短期国库券（T-bills）满足不断增长的融资需求。 不过，市场对于调整的时间和力度仍存在分歧。部分华尔街机构预计，财政部本周可能直接宣布削减长债发行；也有机构认为，更可能出现的是政策指引转向灵活，实际发行规模暂时不会改变。与此同时，短债融资占比持续上升，也让财政部面临新的市场承接能力考验。 长债发行政策可能松动，20年期和30年期国债成焦点 彭博社报道称，华尔街交易商正为美国财政部可能推出2024年初以来最大规模的国债发行政策调整做准备。自2024年1月以来，财政部一直维持相对稳定的中长期国债发行指引，承诺未来数个季度保持票据和债券发行规模不变。 但这一政策可能在11月4日周三公布的季度再融资声明中出现变化。 多家一级交易商预计，财政部将调整现有政策措辞，为2027年削减长期国债发行规模打开空间，同时通过增加国库券和较短期限国债发行弥补融资缺口。 花旗的预测更为激进。该行预计，财政部可能从本月开始削减20年期和30年期国债发行规模，这意味着实际上将偏离此前季度再融资声明中维持发行规模稳定的政策指引。 贝森特近期的操作也令市场提高了对政策转向的警惕。就在上一轮季度再融资计划公布一周后，财政部意外扩大了国债回购规模，被市场视为对长期收益率急剧攀升的回应。 Insight Investment投资专家主管April LaRusse认为，单靠回购计划难以对市场产生足够大的影响。她指出，如果财政部希望压低收益率，而发行政策又是其最主要的工具，那么调整国债发行结构才是更直接的办法。 贝森特对收益率仍有顾虑，但长债收益率已从高位回落 推动市场重新评估财政部发行策略的一个重要背景，是贝森特对美国长期国债收益率水平表现出的不适。 今年10月初，美国长期国债收益率一度升至20多年来最高水平，引发市场对政府融资成本、债务可持续性以及长期国债需求的担忧。贝森特随后扩大国债回购操作，进一步强化了市场对财政部可能通过债务管理手段影响收益率的预期。 不过，财政部本周是否会采取大幅调整行动，仍取决于近期市场环境。自10月初高点以来，长期美债收益率已经有所回落，但彭博指出，截至上周五，30年期美债收益率仍在5.30%以上，接近贝森特今年8月扩大回购操作时的水平。 因此，尽管收益率已从高位回落，财政部对长期融资成本的顾虑并未完全消退。 短债融资占比升至22%，持续依赖国库券的风险上升 如果财政部选择削减长期国债发行，最直接的替代方案将是进一步增加短期国库券发行。 但这一融资策略并非没有代价。美国政府每年财政赤字约2万亿美元，公共债务持续增加，在中长期国债发行规模长期保持稳定的情况下，财政部越来越依赖短期国库券填补融资缺口。 截至9月，国库券在美国未偿市场化国债中的占比已经升至约22%，超过美国财政部借款咨询委员会（TBAC）2024年建议的长期平均20%水平。 短期国库券的期限最长不超过一年，到期后需要频繁滚动发行，意味着财政部必须持续获得投资者承接。美国财政部目前每周拍卖的国库券规模已经超过5000亿美元，上周更创下8390亿美元的纪录。 这也使得美国财政部面临两难：增加短债发行可以暂时避免扩大长期国债供给，但短债占比继续攀升，可能逐渐考验投资者的承接能力，并使政府融资更加容易受到市场流动性变化的影响。 摩根大通策略师此前指出，考虑到美国未来数年庞大的融资需求，以及国库券需求已经出现初步放缓的迹象，削减长期国债发行并不是审慎的选择。财政部官员此前曾将稳定币视为国库券需求的新来源，但目前稳定币带来的国债购买需求尚未形成足够规模。 华尔街对调整幅度存在分歧，摩根大通预计明年8月前维持发行规模不变 尽管不少交易商预计财政部将调整发行指引，但华尔街各大机构对政策变化的时间和力度并未形成共识。 瑞银美国利率策略主管Phoebe White认为，本周更可能出现的是政策指引调整，而不是立即改变实际发行规模。瑞银预计，财政部至少到明年5月之前都不会调整实际发行规模。 巴克莱策略师团队则建议，财政部将原有指引中的“至少未来数个季度”改为“未来数个季度”，从而为调整发行时间和期限结构提供更大灵活性。 这一措辞变化看似细微，却可能意味着财政部不再承诺在未来数个季度维持发行规模稳定，而是为根据市场需求和融资状况灵活调整发行结构留下空间。 摩根大通的判断相对保守。该行策略师团队预计，财政部将继续保留维持未来数个季度发行规模稳定的政策表述，并将这一指引延续至2027年。按照其预测，国债拍卖规模将至少维持不变至明年8月，之后才开始逐步增加，新增发行主要集中在2年至10年期国债。 摩根大通的预测与不少交易商预期的政策转向形成对比。美国银行、高盛和瑞银等机构均在关注财政部是否会调整现有指引。 值得注意的是，现行发行指引的核心框架由前财政部长耶伦确立，2024年1月以来一直延续至今。财政部今年8月已经释放过调整信号，将此前有关未来可能增加票据和浮息债发行的措辞，微妙地调整为评估未来可能发生的发行规模变化。 国债回购政策也将迎来更新，财政部寻求扩大债务管理工具 除了国债发行规模和期限结构，市场还将关注财政部本周对国债回购计划的最新表态。 今年8月，美国财政部宣布，将10年至20年期以及20年至30年期国债的流动性支持回购操作单次规模上限至少翻倍，从20亿美元提高至40亿美元，并于9月9日起实施，持续至11月4日。彭博报道称，财政部近期还将相关回购规模提高至每次60亿美元。 市场普遍预计，财政部将继续维持较高的回购规模，同时保留根据市场情况调整的空间。 高盛策略师团队认为，如果财政部明确将回购纳入管理未偿国债期限结构的政策工具箱，可能进一步增强回购操作对市场的影响力，也可能为财政部在回购操作中降低对价格敏感度创造条件。 此外，市场还将密切关注美国财政部借款咨询委员会（TBAC）的讨论结果。该委员会由投资者、一级交易商及其他市场参与者组成，为财政部提供债务管理建议。本次会议有关市场能否继续消化更大规模国库券发行的反馈，尤其值得关注。 对于本周的季度再融资计划，如果财政部维持现有发行规模不变，下周三场基准国债拍卖总额将达到1250亿美元，其中包括： 11月9日：580亿美元3年期国债； 11月10日：420亿美元10年期国债； 11月12日：250亿美元30年期国债。 美国财政部将于11月4日周三公布季度再融资声明及相关政策文件。对于市场而言，此次声明的关键不仅在于是否调整具体拍卖规模，更在于财政部是否正式改变长期以来维持中长期国债发行稳定的政策框架，以及未来将如何在长期融资成本、短期债务滚动风险和市场承接能力之间取得平衡。 风险提示及免责条款
